how-to-teach-digital-literacy-to-kids:
Digital literacy is not knowing how to use a device. Most children manage that without help and frequently better than the adults teaching them. It is knowing where something came from, who made it, and what they get from you seeing it.

Four questions, taught as habits

Everything below is a version of the same four, introduced at whatever age they land.

Who made this? Not the account that shared it. The person or organisation that produced it originally, which is often several steps back and sometimes unfindable, and unfindable is itself information.

What do they get out of me seeing it? Money, attention, a vote, a belief, a click. Almost nothing arrives for free, and asking this out loud in front of a child a few dozen times installs it permanently.

How do they know? Applied to any claim. Did they see it, measure it, or hear it from somebody who heard it.

Why am I seeing this now? The algorithm question, and the one children find genuinely interesting. Something decided this should be in front of you rather than something else.

Roughly by age

Five to seven. That adverts exist and are trying to make you want something. Point them out on screens and in the street. That is the whole curriculum at this age and it is a good one.

Eight to eleven. That anybody can put anything online. That videos can be edited and pictures changed. That people are paid to recommend things. Start asking who made this about ordinary things, not as a test.

Eleven to fourteen. How feeds decide what to show. Why things that make people angry travel furthest. What sponsored means. How to check a claim in two minutes. Reverse image search, which children love because it feels like a trick.

Fourteen and up. That two honest people can look at the same evidence and disagree. What a primary source is. Why a headline and the study underneath it often do not match. And that generated images and audio now exist and are convincing.

The exercise that works best

Look at something together and be wrong in front of them.

Take a claim you both find plausible, look into it, and let the investigation go where it goes, including to you having believed something incorrect. A child who watches an adult check something and change their mind learns more about how belief should work than from any amount of instruction.

What to avoid

Framing it as everything online is a lie, which is both false and produces a cynic rather than a thinker. The aim is not distrust; it is calibrated trust, which is harder and more useful.

Also avoid making it a lecture attached to their entertainment. Ask about things you are watching, not only about things they chose.

The part that is about them

Digital literacy includes what they produce. That anything sent can be kept and forwarded. That being unkind is easier at a distance and lands the same. That a private account is private from the public and not from a friend with a camera.

The goal is a child who pauses before believing and before posting. Those are the same habit, pointed in two directions.
how-to-prepare-children-for-an-ai-future:
Nobody knows which jobs will exist. Anybody telling you otherwise is guessing, and the confident predictions of ten years ago have aged badly: the tasks assumed safest, writing and drawing, turned out to be among the first affected, while plumbing did not move.

So the honest version of this question is not what should my child learn to be employable. It is what holds its value regardless, and that question does have answers.

What appears to hold

Judgement. Deciding what is worth doing, which of several adequate answers is right here, when something feels off. These systems produce options; somebody still has to choose, and choosing well is a developmental capacity built by making decisions from early on.

Knowing enough to spot a wrong answer. This one is counterintuitive and important. A tool that produces confident, fluent, sometimes-wrong output is dangerous in the hands of somebody with no knowledge of their own. Deep knowledge becomes more valuable, not less, because it is what allows you to catch the failure.

Sitting with a problem that does not resolve. The capacity to stay with something unresolved is exactly what an always-available adequate answer erodes, and it is the precondition for original work.

Working with people. Reading a room, disagreeing without damage, being trusted. None of this is automatable and all of it is built in ordinary childhood.

Physical competence. Hands that can do things. Widely underrated in these conversations and among the least affected.

Knowing what you actually want. A person with no view of their own is easy to steer, and there has never been more steering available.

What probably does not help

Teaching a specific tool, because the tools change. Coding as insurance, which is a poor reason though a fine hobby. Speed, which machines win. And accumulating credentials on the assumption that the ladder stays where it is.

What this means on an ordinary Tuesday

Almost nothing exotic, which is the point.

Let them make real decisions and live with them. Let them be bored, because the gap before invention is where original thought starts. Let them get properly good at something slowly, so they know what depth feels like. Protect the reading, because knowledge is what catches errors. Give them work with their hands. And let difficulty stand rather than removing it, which is the single hardest thing on this list for a parent who can now remove almost any difficulty in seconds.

The sentence worth saying to them

Your child is not in a race with these systems and does not need to beat them at anything. The useful position is not being faster than a machine; it is being the person who decides what the machine should be pointed at, and who notices when the output is wrong.

That is a developmental achievement rather than a technical one, and it is built the same way it always was.
future-skills-every-child-needs:
Most future skills lists are the same handful of competencies renamed every few years. Here are the ones with genuine developmental backing, and the age at which each becomes something you can actually build rather than merely hope for.

Attention that a child controls

Buildable from around four, seriously from six. Not the ability to sit still, which is different. The ability to choose what to attend to and return after drifting. Built by protected stretches of self-chosen absorption and eroded by constant interruption. Everything else on this list depends on it.

Tolerating difficulty

From about five, and it takes a decade. Staying with something that is not working. This is now the most quietly endangered capacity on the list, because a good-enough answer is always available. It is built by being allowed to struggle with a person nearby rather than a person taking over.

Judgement

From about seven, properly from eleven. Choosing between options that are all defensible. Built only by making real decisions with real consequences, in small reversible doses long before the stakes rise. A child who has never chosen badly has not practised choosing.

Deep knowledge of something

From about eight. Not general knowledge. One area known properly, whatever it is. It teaches what depth feels like, which is transferable, and it is what allows somebody to notice when a confident answer is wrong.

Reading difficult things

From about nine. Holding an argument across pages, following something that does not resolve in a paragraph. Built by volume first, then by being read to above their level for years longer than feels necessary.

Working with people who are not like you

From four, continuously. Disagreeing without damage, repairing, being trusted. Built in unsupervised play and in groups an adult did not curate.

Making something with your hands

Any age. Cooking, building, repairing, growing, an instrument. Underrated in these lists, least affected by automation, and it teaches that the world is manipulable rather than only consumable.

Knowing what you want

From eleven, and it needs room. A view of your own. Built by being asked what you think and having the answer taken seriously, including when it is inconvenient.

What is missing from this list on purpose

Coding, which is a good hobby and a poor insurance policy. Public speaking, which is a useful skill rather than a foundational capacity. Creativity as a standalone item, because it is what happens when knowledge, attention and tolerance for difficulty are all present rather than something trainable on its own.

And anything with a brand name attached.

Every item here is built by ordinary childhood done unhurriedly. That is not a comforting coincidence; it is why these are the ones that last.
ai-vs-human-intelligence-what-should-chi:
The comparison is usually framed as a competition, which is the wrong frame and produces bad decisions. A more useful question is what each is actually for.

What these systems do well

Pattern completion at enormous scale. Producing fluent text on demand. Summarising. Translating. Generating many options quickly. Recalling and recombining what has already been written. Working without tiring, at three in the morning, without embarrassment.

That last one matters more than it sounds. A patient explainer that never sighs is genuinely valuable to a child who is ashamed of not understanding.

What they cannot do

Know whether they are right. There is no internal check. Fluency and accuracy are produced by the same process, which is why the wrong answers sound exactly like the right ones.

Want anything. No stake, no preference, nothing at risk. They cannot tell you what matters because nothing matters to them.

Encounter the world. No body, no consequences, no memory of yesterday. They have read about grief and rain and have met neither.

Take responsibility. When it is wrong, a person carries it. That is not a technical gap that will close; responsibility requires somebody who can be held to it.

What follows for a child

Not that they should avoid these tools, and not that they should out-compete them at summarising. The tasks worth building are the ones on the second list.

Knowing things properly, because knowledge is what lets you catch a confident error.

Judging, because output is not a decision.

Caring about something, because that is what supplies direction.

Being present to actual life, because that is the material everything else works on.

The thing to be careful of when talking about this

Two failure modes, and both are common in adults.

The first is dismissal. Saying it is just autocomplete and nothing to worry about. Children can see it is useful and conclude you are uninformed, which ends the conversation.

The second is awe. Talking about it as though it thinks and knows, which builds a mental model that makes a child trust it in the places it is least trustworthy.

The accurate version sits between and is more interesting than either: a remarkable tool, built by people, which produces language extremely well and understands nothing.

What is worth saying to a teenager

That the value of a person was never their ability to produce a competent paragraph on demand, and that anybody who built their sense of themselves on being able to do that is having a difficult decade.

What has not moved is knowing something deeply, deciding what is worth doing, and being answerable for it.

Your child does not need to compete with a machine. They need to become the kind of person who knows what to do with one.
